“[This movie is] the idea that we’re all animals. We’re all part of this ecosystem together,” Chong tells Deadline. “I feel like when we center ourselves as animals, it reminds you that we all have a stake in this together, we all have a responsibility to all of it together. I don’t know if people, even better yet, children, carry that into their lives. I think that could be a powerful thing. So, if there’s one thing people do take away, I hope it’s that.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Below, Chong talks with Deadline about blending humor with social justice issues, the challenges of bringing the natural world to life and entering his sage-advice era at Pixar.

DEADLINE: OK, take me back to the early stages. How did Hoppers come about? Did you have to pitch it to Pixar, or did you already have a script?

DANIEL CHONG: It was just me at the time. I came in empty-handed after [completing his Cartoon Network show] We Bare Bears . I didn’t really have any ideas. Eventually, I pitched this idea, and at that time it was called Penguin Avatar , and I didn't think they were going to pick it. I was like, "This is just a funny pitch. This is the get-a-laugh pitch, and then we'll move on." But six years later, we made the movie. We just had to substitute penguins for beavers, but that was the gist. Then Jesse Andrews came in and wrote Hoppers with me.

DEADLINE: That still sounds like a hard idea to get people on board with. What do you think worked?

CHONG: The joke that this is like Avatar was in that pitch because it felt like just an easy way to clue people in into what we were parroting a little bit, but also let them know you're going to think it's Avatar , but it's totally not [laughs]. That was a big one. The other was just the idea that there was this opportunity to go into the animal world and feel the inner life of these animals. That was something Pixar hadn’t quite done specifically in this animal world, and I think that’s what sold it and why it appealed to them.

DEADLINE: How did you and Jesse talk through making the script?

CHONG: Without a script and just an outline, we had a sense of where we wanted to go with it, but we worked very fluidly with how we created the story. That’s why the movie is so freeform. We wanted it to be very organic and unexpected. We didn’t want the audience to feel the structure of it. And if you think about it, Mission: Impossible and those bigger action-type movies are built that way. They are built around crazy set pieces, unexpected twists and turns. So, I just knew that one of the last things that I wanted to do was work on this in a linear way.

When Jesse came on, he had the tough task of working the way I wanted to work, which was just out of order. He would write something in Act 2, then go to Act 1, then jump to Act 3. We went around and around, putting up reels in a hodgepodge way, and then started shaping it to make sense. It’s madness to work that way, but it made the movie what it is because I think that was the only way we could go so wild and take so many swings in so many parts of the movie. We had an anarchic way of our process.

DEADLINE: Using wild animals seems to be the throughline of your filmography so far. What speaks to you about using these creatures to tell your stories?

CHONG: There's an inherent charm in seeing animals anthropomorphized that has always appealed to me. And doing this in animation adds a level of surrealness that everyone can still easily connect and relate to. The humor and silliness come pretty easily from there, but it will also allow me to venture into some weightier topics while still keeping things fun, because at the end of the day, it’s a stack of bears and a beaver with a crown.

DEADLINE: And what about the robotic portion of the premise? This could have just been about regular animals saving their habitat.

CHONG: I think that came from my interest in robot animals. I was reading a lot about animatronics, and A.I. wasn’t quite what it is today, but it was definitely building its way into the zeitgeist. So, I was reading a lot about robotics. I learned in some documentaries that they actually put robot animals into nature to spy on them, and they have cameras in their eyes. If no one has seen them, they are up on YouTube, and you can watch them. They are incredible and a little cheesy looking, and I don’t mean that in a bad way, because robotics are amazing, but they don’t look like real animals [laughs]. When you see them, you look and say, there’s no way an animal is going to buy this, but then the animals poke and prod it, probably questioning whether it’s a friend or a foe. So, I was imagining: What if that technology was so good, the animals could not tell the difference? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: Since Hoppers was released in March, there’s still so much online discourse about the absurdist, playfully dark humor that you all managed to get into the film that hasn’t really been done before in the Disney/Pixar canon. How would you describe your comedic sensibilities?

CHONG: I grew up with a lot of pop culture. I was a kid raised on movies, TV, and comic strips. I loved Garfield , Calvin and Hobbes , Far Side –I read that a lot as a kid, and I owned every book. I remember recently looking back at it, looking through the jokes, and I was like, “Oh my God, this is our movie.” It’s similar to our anthropomorphic animals. It's a little bit satirical. It's very absurd. And it just felt like that language was really what I grew up on.

And because I’m a kid of the ’80s, I love early Tim Burton, just really weird, strange, and tonally off-kilter movies that you can’t even put in a box. Is it horror? Is it comedy? Is it action? And that’s the kind of mind meld that my brain was exposed to growing up with all these things. So, I just brought that into Hoppers, thinking about all these genres. I just wanted it to be all those things.

DEADLINE: I want to break some of these comedic beats down. You’ve got Diane, the shark, who is hoisted up on a highway by the avian creatures to help squish the mayor to death. In a post-credits scene, you’ve got the animals playing with another character's face mask. There’s so much. What was the thing you had to fight for the most or stick to your guns about?

CHONG: Listen, we had to fight for everything [laughs]. I want to be clear that the studio was behind a lot of it, but we did get a lot of notes. And because Pixar has been around for a very long time, it was a lot of, “Is this a Pixar movie? Is this what we are going to make?”

DEADLINE: There’s truly nothing like it.

CHONG: I think that’s because there’s a sense of humor that’s a little bit chaotic and illogical. Pixar movies are built so much on logic in a lot of ways. There was a freeness in the humor that many people were unsure about. For example, when they saw the animals with crowns, even if you start with something as simple as that, I think an older Pixar might have noted the situation to death. It would have been something like, “OK, why do those animals have crowns? Explain it to me. So, they just have them? Well, we have to know where they got it from.” So, you would get questions to logic out all these decisions. But now, it’s kind of about explaining that something like that would ruin the joke, and it shouldn’t be explained where the crowns come from. So, if we liked something enough, the work was on us; we just had to figure out how to get it through so it didn’t trip up the audience when they watched it.

So, instead, we came up with that joke where one of the scientists goes, "Where'd they get those little crowns?" And this other scientist goes, "Is that your question?" And that was our way of just going like, "We know this is crazy. We know it doesn't make sense, but it's all crazy, so go with it."

And I think once you're starting to train the audience to go on this ride of craziness and absurdness, I think then you get them to a place where a shark gets raised into the sky with some birds, and you just go, "OK, I guess that's the natural conclusion to this movie." And faces getting ripped off. I would say the only issue was sometimes it got a little scary for kids when we did audience previews, which we didn't know until the end of the making of this movie. So we had to tweak a couple scenes, but overall, I think I got everything I wanted in there [laughs]. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: I’m still in shock that the killing of the butterfly made it in. It was the only thing I heard people talking about. And the reactions in the screenings I went to? People were screaming. Talk about how that scene came about and what was your experience watching it with others?

CHONG: I love talking about it. Honestly, having a movie and getting to know that that is going to happen and everyone is going to react a little differently is one of the funnest parts about this movie, especially watching it in a theater. I remember when we were in audience previews, Pete Docter [CCO of Pixar] turned to me and was like, "That's why we go to the theater to have moments like that." And he's right. Like you said, you got to experience that with the crowd, because they're looking around going, "Did that happen?" And they need somebody to validate it, so they can laugh because it's so crazy.

We had the idea for this scene pretty early on, though in our story discussions. We did something like eight internal screenings on the movie, to vet it with our own studio. Even I thought it was going to get cut because it was just a joke that we put in that was funny for now, but come on, there's no way we can do it.

But all the credit goes to the people up at Pixar, like Pete Docter and Andrew Stanton , who were like, “That is staying in the movie. We are not changing that.” And they protected the scene. We never got a note on it. So it made it all the way to the end with no problems. We got more notes on the shark than that [laughs].

CHONG: Yeah, I think it’s because Pixar knew they had something good with that moment and they wanted to protect it. When they took it to audience previews, they saw that the audience loved it. And it's such a pivotal point for the movie because it's when the movie turns and you start running down a hill and you can't stop. And that's the sensation I wanted with that squish. And Meryl Streep was incredible with it. I was afraid she would say no to the role because she wouldn't be around past her only scene, but she got the joke and was game. So everything about it was just…I could talk about it forever, but I love it.

DEADLINE: We’ve talked a lot about the humor, but let’s get into the emotions. There’s a lot of heartfelt material there too. What scene made you more emotional than you anticipated after you finished making it?

CHONG: The scene with Mabel when she breaks down to George and says, "I'm so tired of fighting alone, doing this alone." I think that line and the way Piper [Curda] delivered it, man, there is just an authenticity. And that’s one of the reasons we hired her; she brought such sincerity to that line. And I feel like, oh, she's speaking for all of us. That is how it feels out here: that we are alone in our battles and in the things we care about. I just felt the connectedness that moment brought.

But the other thing is that we added a moment at the end of the movie, and it was the last thing we animated because we needed people to love Mabel even more. It’s when Mabel returns to live with her grandmother before she dies, her parents leave, and Mabel decides to stay with her grandma. So, she lives and takes care of her and feeds her and brushes her hair and becomes a caretaker in the last days, months, years of her life. I remember when we added that, that was everything. It really tied together her love for her grandma and for this place, the glade, they shared together. And that part gets me every time I see it.

DEADLINE: The animation of the water, the glade and fires is gorgeous. What was the most challenging depiction and how did you get through the other side?

CHONG: It’s funny because the whole movie was this whole, like “How are we going to do this?” To be honest, the reason this movie exists is because of my naivete and my inexperience in making CG films. My producer always tells me, "If you knew how hard these movies are to make, you would not have made this film, because there were so many things like fire, water, and all these effects and crowds that logically you would never put together.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

But to answer your question. It was that dam breaking at the end of the movie. There was no bigger technical challenge than breaking that thing apart, with all those crowds on it, all that water flowing down, and then taking out the fire. The effects, the set, the cinematography—nightmare. [Laughs.]

DEADLINE: Not to add to your PTSD, but how did you get through that?

CHONG: Luckily, we had a great team. I can’t take too much credit. These are typical teams at Pixar who are just excellent at what they do. Also, they came off of Elemental , so they were like, "OK, well, we've been through that. We have some experience with some elements.” They know complexity, and they rallied together.

DEADLINE: What was the most important theme for you to get through in this movie? There’s a lot of environmentalism, isolation, togetherness. What do you want people to resonate with most?

CHONG: Two things. The first thing I would say from a Mabel standpoint is the power of community. We brought on a bunch of environmental organizers. There were young 20-year-olds just like Mabel who we brought on to show the movie, and to get notes and feedback from them to make sure it was authentic to their experience as activists. And a lot of the way that they would describe what helped them endure in the fight for the things that they cared about was community, was having other people there to fight with.

And that is Mabel's biggest issue: she's alone in the fight until she learns to connect with other people, learns to talk with them and bring them in, as opposed to pushing them away. And that is the thing that all the activists really connected with. And that's why at the end of the movie, we have her connecting with those scientists because that's going to be her community from now on. And of course, she's got George.

The other thing I wanted to throw out there is the idea that we’re all animals. We’re all part of this ecosystem together. And I feel like when we center ourselves as animals, it reminds you that, oh, we all have a stake in all of this together, and we all have a responsibility to all of it together. I don’t know if people, even better yet, children, carry that into their lives. I think that could be a powerful thing. So, if there’s one thing people do take away, I hope it’s that.

DEADLINE: So, what’s next for you after this massive undertaking?

CHONG: I’m getting more embedded into helping Pixar’s future. So, they now have me as an executive producer on one of their upcoming films, Ghost Market . I’m excited. If anyone liked Hoppers , they will love Ghost Market. It is a huge swing. It is unexpected. It's full of crazy things. Our writer, Jesse Andrews, is co-directing it, along with one of my good friends, Trevor Jimenez, and they are cooking up something incredible. And I'm so happy I get to be along for the ride with them, and I get to be a mentor and share my experiences making a movie with them, as they are first-time directors. There are some other projects at the studio that I’m giving feedback and notes on, and I’m also back in development, and they want an idea, so we’ll see what that is. But to be fair, they aren’t rushing me [laughs].

I like that I can take a moment just to focus on helping other people, and it’s such a gift to share the things I know with other people and guide other people. It’s a totally different skill set to encourage people as much as you can without overstepping, and to help them be the best they can be.

articles.title: Solo Leveling Doesn't Deserve the Hype Because of One Fatal Flaw
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of A-1 Pictures Even before the anime debuted in 2024, Solo Leveling was globally popular thanks to the exceptional story written by Chugong. The light novel and the webtoon’s success, along with the stunning visuals by A-1 Pictures, made it possible for the anime adaptation to reach new heights of popularity. While the novel and the webtoon are already concluded, […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Even before the anime debuted in 2024, Solo Leveling was globally popular thanks to the exceptional story written by Chugong. The light novel and the webtoon’s success, along with the stunning visuals by A-1 Pictures, made it possible for the anime adaptation to reach new heights of popularity. While the novel and the webtoon are already concluded, the anime still has a huge chunk of story left to adapt. The second season was released in Winter last year, and it wasn't until July this year that a sequel movie was announced . While fans know almost nothing about the anime sequel, the only thing that's confirmed at this point is that it's going to be another massive success.

However, while the series has countless fans, the number of haters can't be ignored either. The series is often criticized for a number of reasons, including the fact that it ignores a lot of character depth, among many other things. For a series as popular as Solo Leveling , it receives just as much hate for always being in the spotlight. Although it’s completely subjective to like or hate the series, it does have its weak points that make the criticisms valid. While Solo Leveling is far from the best series , it’s not nearly as boring as many would claim it to be. However, there is one fatal flaw that makes the series deserving of its overhyped reputation.

There's no denying that Solo Leveling 's world-building could have been one of the best in the webtoon industry. The story takes place in an urban fantasy world where mysterious gates showed up out of nowhere. As if that wasn’t enough, it also blends video game rules through the system , which is directly tied to the historic event that changed the world. While the main story itself takes place in a realistic setting, Jinwoo often travels through dimensions to level up, which is why we keep seeing all kinds of different settings.

Not only that, but the world-building continues to expand after he uncovers the secret about the System. The story features the world through his lens and tries its best to focus on the juxtaposition of the modern setting and the alternate fantasy realms that are directly tied to it. In theory, the world-building seems flawless, but the story barely manages to hold up to its true potential. The initial idea behind the world-building was great, but somewhere between the fast-paced story and the intense action, the world-building never truly had a chance to shine.

World-building is more than just the setting of the story and the places it features, but it also includes the history, society, characters, the power system, and more. Whether it's the historic cosmic war or the side characters, the series could have done a lot with the world-building, but never truly had the opportunity. Whether it's a real-world setting with gates, monsters, and guilds, it's obvious that all these things were only there for surface-level build-up. It also doesn't help that the story focuses way too much on Jinwoo, even to the point of neglecting just about any other character besides him. This includes the villains and the supporting characters since rarely anyone had the chance to shine with Jinwoo grabbing all the attention.

Solo Leveling relies on a straightforward story with lots of action , the protagonist’s power-up, and the constant threat he keeps facing. The only reason the series actually works is that it's a simplistic portrayal of an urban fantasy that doesn’t try to appear too deep or complex. It’s the kind of show you can read or watch for fun without thinking too deeply about the state of the world and characters. Because the story is fast-paced, the viewers' attention remains on the protagonist, so you wouldn't expect much from the political intrigue and the social setting it introduced.

Instead of focusing on heavy lore, the series relies on methodical progression to help Jinwoo reach the top as soon as possible. The only redeeming quality that sets Solo Leveling apart from other series is the intense battles Jinwoo has fought throughout his journey. As an action series, it nails the fight choreography even in the webtoon thanks to the incredible illustrations by DUBU. However, the animation studio elevates them even further with fluid sequences as it relies on the story's only strength. It's not really surprising that Solo Leveling is the best when it comes to webtoon adaptations, and it’s easily the best series from A-1 Pictures studio.

Do you think Solo Leveling could have been even better without this fatal flaw? In your opinion, what is the one thing the series is missing the most? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

articles.title: Kevin Feige Explains the Best Place to Find Accurate Doomsday Spoilers, And It's an MCU First

Fresh off the new trailer for the film, and rumors that are as endless as the multiverse itself, Marvel fans are […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google We're three weeks away from the release of Avengers: Doomsday , and even though we're closer every day some fans still want to find the Marvel spoilers , luckily Kevin Feige has a compass for you. Fresh off the new trailer for the film , and rumors that are as endless as the multiverse itself, Marvel fans are still trying to predict what will happen next in the big crossover movie, even if it means finding out ahead of time how right they are. Speaking to this elusive hunt, Feige revealed the best place for it, and it's exactly where you think.

“If you wanted spoilers for The Odyssey , you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for Doomsday and Secret Wars , you can go look at the comics ,” Feige told EW . “It is very much the same thing that we’re doing, which is the fun of what happens in the culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event, and what Doctor Doom does next. And that very much is what Secret Wars is.” Though Feige's clear sense of telling fans what to do on their spoiler hunt should seem like common sense, it's a pretty astounding confirmation from Feige since the MCU rarely recommends that fans pick up the comics.

Though the Marvel Cinematic Universe is built on decades of comic book stories and the work of thousands of writers and artists, it very seldom acknowledges that history in any meaningful way. Films in the series may share the same name as major storylines from the comics, like The Winter Soldier , Civil War , and Infinity War , but what ends up executed on-screen often takes on a totally different form compared to what readers saw when they picked up the comic books themselves.

For Feige to say that spoilers for both Doomsday and Secret Wars can be found in the comics themselves may indicate that some actual key moments from the series will happen in the narrative and not just visual recreations of iconic covers . Some of the big swings that happen in the pages of Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić's 2015 miniseries that could end up on the big screen are: heroes being put on a lifeboat to escape the final incursion, Doctor Doom killing Thanos in a confrontation, the formation of the Thor Corps as enforcers for Doom's will on Battleworld, and God Emperor Doom's subjugation of the Fantastic Four heroes after remaking the world from the pieces of the multiverse.

Perhaps the biggest spoiler from the Secret Wars comic that feels like the most obvious spoiler for the movie is the actual ending of the story. By the conclusion of the series, the multiverse is slowly being rebuilt, but the main continuity of Marvel comics has been established as "Earth Prime" rather than "Earth-616." Given that we already know Marvel's plans for the X-Men will kick off the next wave of movies after Secret Wars, and Black Panther III is in that first slate as well, an all-new Earth that "resets" the MCU is inevitable, and it's been in comic book store shelves for a decade.

articles.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum Wraps Filming & Reveals a Hilarious New Set Video
articles.summary: Warner Bros. The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum has officially completed production, and the film is commemorating that achievement in the perfect way. Rather than posting the typical production wrap announcement on social media, director Andy Serkis and the team behind The Hunt for Gollum kept things meta, posting a production video that treats […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum has officially completed production, and the film is commemorating that achievement in the perfect way. Rather than posting the typical production wrap announcement on social media, director Andy Serkis and the team behind The Hunt for Gollum kept things meta, posting a production video that treats Gollum as if he were the actual celebrity star of the film. The results are about as hilarious as you would imagine.

Needless to say, Gollum – the creature whose centuries-long obsession helped determine the fate of Middle-earth – is not one to give up his squatter's rights so easily. So even though the sets and performer trailers start getting broken down and taken away, Gollum isn't quite ready to go.

That’s a wrap! Well, almost. Production on The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum has officially ended. Only in theaters December 2027. pic.twitter.com/mBb1Rmw70J

Andy Serkis is a madman. His early 2000s performance as Gollum in the original The Lord of the Rings trilogy redefined what motion-capture performance was capable of and introduced an iconic character to cinema. Now, decades later, Serkis is getting to return to LotR as a full-fledged filmmaker, occupying the director's chair even as he reprises his role as Gollum.

The Hunt for Gollum is a prequel set before and during the events of The Fellowship of the Ring , told from Gollum's perspective. According to J.R.R. Tolkien's lore, Gollum set out to hunt down Bilbo Baggins after the events of The Hobbit . After serving the giant spider Shelob for a time, Gollum is captured by Sauron and tortured until he reveals that Bilbo has the ring, making Sauron aware of Hobbits and the Shire for the first time. The story continues with Gollum escaping Sauron's clutches, only to be hunted by Gandalf and Strider (aka Aragorn), who are also looking to confirm Gandalf's suspicions about Biblo's ring. The film is said to end with Gollum turning the tables and going on the hunt after learning about Frodo Baggins and his quest to destroy the One Ring. Supposedly, it will end with Gollum picking up the Fellowship's trail as they enter the Mines of Moria.

Obviously, this lore is well known to anyone who has been a Tolkien fan. But what's especially interesting about the production wrap video above is that it hints that the filmmakers understand that what will set this film apart is the character of Gollum, and all the wild charisma he brings to the table. This video is probably the first of many we'll see with "Gollum" doing his own press, and we're here for it.

Andy Serkis is long overdue for proper acclaim for his performance-capture creation, and if Gollum successfully carries his own Lord of the Rings film, there will be little room left to debate if performance-capture acting deserves the same consideration (and awards) as traditional performance.

The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum will be in theaters on December 17, 2027.

articles.content:
Zyri , who voiced the titular character in " Steven Universe " and played Brian Corbett on "The Goldbergs," has come out as trans. In a Substack post on Wednesday, Zyri wrote about the challenges of being a child star and coming to terms with their gender identity.

"Coming to terms with my dysphoria and my transness was only a small piece of my journey towards being a whole, authentic person, but it was notable as the first thing that truly felt like mine in my entire life," Zyri wrote. "That’s also why for a time I was so terrified of being outed: I didn’t want to lose my newfound light the way I’d lost control of my name, my childhood, and my entire identity to the brand I was molded into by others. I know now that I really had nothing to fear there — the only thing that defines me is me — but I’ve had to continuously unlearn being afraid of losing all of myself again. That’s probably something I’ll have to remind myself of for the rest of my life, but at least now, for the very first time, I can envision the rest of my life. I celebrated my twenty-eighth birthday just over a year ago now, and the symbolic nature of that number shouldn’t be lost on anyone who grew up like I did. What twenty-one year old me would’ve cynically viewed as being past my cosmically-assigned expiration date, is now something that truly feels worth celebrating. articles.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed as Storm Descends on Northeast
articles.summary: The annual event is one of the most-watched TV events of the year for NBC.
articles.content:
In an unprecedented move, the 100th edition of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City will be postponed until Saturday Nov. 28, a source familiar with the matter confirms to The Hollywood Reporter .

The decision comes as a powerful nor'easter storm is bearing down on the northeast, with potential wind gusts north of 60 miles per hour.

It's also a major headache for the broadcast partner NBC , with last year's parade drawing over 34 million viewers between NBC and Peacock.

The parade has never been canceled in its 100 years, though some of the iconic giant balloons have been grounded when there have been high winds. This year's postponement is also a first. articles.title: With HBO Series 'Scams for a Better Tomorrow,' Oobah Butler Has a Language for Your Frustration
articles.summary: The former Vice provocateur's five-part HBO series cons the wellness, tech and music industries to help make viewers "feel less f***ing insane" in modern times.
articles.content:
Is Oobah Butler a journalist or a satirist? The latest voice to step up in HBO's many forays into news-like programming doesn't seem to know himself. Perhaps he’s both: the 34-year-old host of the new five-part series Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow has carved out his own niche in the loose structure that cable TV news has taken on of late. The bleach-blond Brit finds a space between black-pill cynicism, cutting satire and actual public service as he holds a mirror up to several industries and cultures, often by mimicking their own languages and modes to show, in the simplest ways, how warped, corrupted or morally bankrupt they have become — or always were. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV 'Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow' Review: Oobah Butler Exposes Modern Life's Many Frauds in Nathan Fielder-esque HBO Comedy Doc Movies Scott Caan Thought He Got a Prank Text. It Was Actually David Fincher Wanting Him in 'Cliff Booth'

"I think the problem is, whenever you try and pin yourself down as one, the other one feels intriguing," Butler told The Hollywood Reporter in an interview this week. "I don't know. I think at the heart of all of it is some sort of truth-seeking. And I'm trying to learn something through using satire, which I think there's a massive tradition of in both of our countries."

Satire may be too light a term for the lengths he goes to. In the series premiere, a deadpan, dead-serious Butler bamboozles the wellness industry, getting entirely too far into the fray as he pitches, focus-groups and activates a skin serum sold as the product of children's tears. In a later episode, he explores the fine line between scamming and marketing by pitching an eager tech industry on a dating app where singles open up to purported AI agents who turn out to be the very users they've matched with. And after that, he handily infiltrates Amazon's rankings and charts with a terrible pop song to expose how hackable the attention economy has become in the TikTok/nepo baby era of late-stage capitalism. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

With the series, which premiered on HBO Max on Sunday, Butler is being introduced to his widest American audience yet. While his aim and agenda are global in scope, they are very much rooted in America, his adopted home for over two years, and its many cultures. Still, it's no stateside debut: As he notes, his résumé includes years writing for Vice Media, the youth media brand whose DIY, parachute style of journalism raised eyebrows in the same ways Oobah is about to. Butler's work during the now once-again-fledgling brand 's globally focused era no doubt earned him some American fans — his articles include "I Became a Fidget Spinner to Try to Understand Fidget Spinning" and "I Turned Bottles of Amazon Drivers' Pee Into a #1 Bestseller" — and the show's first-person style has the feel of an offshoot of the Emmy-winning Vice on HBO.

In 2013, that show took Dennis Rodman to North Korea to meet Kim Jong Un for some basketball diplomacy. While Butler, more than a decade later, doesn't quite top that bizarre feat in his initial run, he does carry the torch, using his charm, wit and an alarmingly natural fearlessness to finagle his way into the top echelons of U.S. industries and get his satirical products in front of some notable gatekeepers, including the New York Times wine critic and Theranos' former chief creative officer. It's a ruse, but it takes the kind of steely nerve that makes great journalism.

In a sense, Butler has been riding the twists and turns of a vastly shifting industry into what's become the perfect career for a modern journalist. He started at 15, carving out a freelance career writing for magazines instead of enrolling at one of the U.K.'s many fine universities. The gonzo style and large-scale efforts to disrupt systems he sees as rigged began early, with a prank website for his fake restaurant, The Shed at Dulwich (shaving cream and dishwasher fluid were pictured as menu items), which he used to game TripAdvisor until it became the No. 1 restaurant in London on the popular travel site. That surprising result launched a career defined by big, flashy, newsmaking satire. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"All of a sudden, I had a kind of, like, encouragement to go and make my work about inauthenticity and manipulation and social engineering," he told THR . "Well, the stuff that I'd always been interested in. And you have a success, and it gives you permission to be like, 'OK, now here's a version of my work that I can get really excited by.'"

A short film, How I Faked My Way to the Top of Paris Fashion Week , followed as Butler went along with Vice and the rest of the startup media world's ill-fated pivot to video. But his schemes, style and sensibility broke through, and soon he leveled up to the major leagues: He was given the hosting job at MTV's Catfish UK and in 2023 he produced a documentary for Channel 4; it was here, he says, that he cut his teeth, learning to produce documentaries under specific standards and practices.

"I'm a disruptor. I like to come up with stuff which is going to make news, make people talk," Butler says in voiceover in the series' first episode. (Spoilers ahead!) Part of this is following his narratives down rabbit holes that lead to the truly unexpected. Cannibalism, for example, is the conclusion of that first episode, and it may leave viewers taken aback, to say the least. ("I didn't realize I'd be a vegetarian and a cannibal, which is fun," he gleefully told THR .) It all gets stranger by the time the big finale episode arrives — a lengthier effort that spanned the time the first four episodes took to produce — as Butler marries into royalty, nearly causes an international scandal (and even gets some new laws on the books) as he takes on what he believes is at the heart of British and American identity. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

With such heights of disruptive newsmaking reached in his first season, what can we possibly expect if the series is picked up for a second run? Like most journalists, Butler doesn't really know what his next story will be. But he is certainly grounded in why he'll be chasing it.

"I'm trying to entertain and to provide people with a language to make themselves feel less fucking insane," he says. "I think we know the world feels rigged in a certain way, and I think it's good to lay that out on the table. I'm constantly learning that you can't trust the systems to protect you, which is a little, little sad. At the very base level, [I want to] give people a language for their frustrations."

articles.title: Tony Romo Lands Post-CBS Gig With Betting App Betr as "Chief Predictions Officer" (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Romo will produce original content and deliver sports predictions for the betting app co-founded by Jake Paul, with his debut set for a Thanksgiving Day campaign.
articles.content:
Tony Romo has landed his first post-CBS media gig… and it's with a sports betting app, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

Betr, the betting and predictions app co-founded by Jake Paul and Joey Levy, says that it has inked a deal with Romo to make him the company's "chief predictions officer." The role is essentially a media play, with Romo appearing in original content, delivering sport-related predictions, and serving as a face of the brand in marketing.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson Is About to Get His Own James Bond Weapon, but You Don't Need to Be 007 to Get Your Hands on One, Too

While this sinks in, there couldn't be a better time to step back into the Bonds of […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google After years of speculation, big changes behind the scenes, and a lot of arguments over exactly who should follow in the footsteps of Daniel Craig, Amazon MGM Studios has finally announced Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond . While this sinks in, there couldn't be a better time to step back into the Bonds of the past with several lots in Heritage Auction's Signature sale , which features weapons brandished by some of those who have already completed their service as the world's best known spy. Pattinson will be the seventh actor to portray the character in an official Bond feature film, but for fans of his most recent predecessors, this auction has something that will put you in double-oh heaven.

Up for auction are some stand-out weapons from Daniel Craig and Pierce Brosnan outings as Bond. This includes a grappling pistol used by Brosnan in GoldenEye , a Walther P99 from Tomorrow Never Dies and Die Another Day , along with a Walther PPK "drop gun" from Craig's Quantum of Solace . All three of the weapons have starting bids of $8,000, but how much they actually sell for will wholly depend on who is bidding when the auction comes to a close at the beginning of December.For many, the most significant of these weapons is the GoldenEye piton grappling pistol from Brosnan's 1995 debut as Bond . Used in the opening sequence of the movie, this was the very first weapon used by Brosnan's Bond during his tenure of the role, and that could make it more significant for Bond collectors looking for that real talking point piece, even though it has undergone some restoration.

It is now five years since Daniel Craig brought his term as Bond to a close in the most spectacular and devastating way possible, bowing out as the character was killed off for the first time in the history of the franchise. This means that the next time we see Bond it will be with a completely fresh start under the direction of Denis Villeneuve for Amazon MGM Studios . Last week, it was finally revealed that Robert Pattinson will be the man stepping into the suave suits and polished shoes of the super spy, but the question still to be answered is what kind of Bond will Pattinson be and how will he compare to the almost flawless run of the Craig era. That is something that we don't know just yet, but with Pattinson's casting now being public, it will not be long before we discover more about the return of Bond in his, appropriately, seventh iteration.

In the meantime, every Bond fan has their favorite version of the character, from the classic and still untouchable Sean Connery original through to Craig's gritty and "real" modern interpretation who broke many bond tropes and long-standing character rules in his five movies. While those movies are constantly being watched by new audiences on streaming, bringing a new actor in can always stir up interest in the older movies of the franchise. Pattinson's casting has certainly got people talking about James Bond again after the long hiatus between Craig's exit and the eventual announcement - with a big change made during that time as the franchise was fully bought out by Amazon MGM Studios. While opinions are currently split over the announcement, with some believing Pattinson is too well known to play Bond and others hailing him as the perfect addition to the line-up, we still have a while to wait before Pattinson finally makes his debut as the character in 2028.

What are your thoughts on the new James Bond casting? Let us know in the comments.
